On the Art of Failing Upward

Let me tell you something no motivational speaker will ever say: failure isn't a teacher. Teachers show up every day whether they want to or not, grading papers at 1 AM while their marriage quietly disintegrates. Failure shows up once, does one dramatic thing—burns down the barn metaphorically—and then sits back waiting for applause as if it built the whole farm.

We've been sold this gorgeous lie that failure leads to success, that every billionaire has a drawer full of rejection letters like trophies. Well, yes, Steve Jobs got fired from Apple. He also had a trust fund, a Stanford education, and an entire culture obsessed with his genius before he was thirty. Try getting fired from a warehouse job in Dayton and see how many venture capitalists knock on your door offering a second chance.

Here's my real complaint though—not everyone gets the luxury of failing spectacularly enough to become interesting. Most people fail in these quiet, unphotogenic ways. They stay in relationships past their expiration date because leaving would mean admitting they were wrong about another human being....

Ah yes, the butterfly effect—or as I prefer to call it, the "I've Really Fucked Up" effect. You know when you're standing in the wreckage of your life, staring at what used to be your carefully constructed plans, and someone gently suggests that maybe that one throwaway comment you made three years ago is why your entire professional network now views you as toxic? That's recognizing the domino effect.

The universe has a sick sense of humor. It loves nothing more than watching us believe we live in straight lines, cause-and-effect being neat little arrows on a whiteboard. Then it waits until we've invested our time, money, dignity, and whatever remaining hair we have left into some venture, before revealing that the whole thing was actually set in motion by something absurdly small: a typo in an email, taking the wrong train once, saying "bless you" instead of "excuse me."

Think about it. Your career trajectory wasn't derailed by a single catastrophic failure—that would be too kind. No, it was a slow-motion catastrophe initiated by you failing to respond to a LinkedIn message from 2014, which created a data point suggesting you were unprofessional, which led to you getting passed over for a promotion, which meant you stayed in a job you hated longer, which prevented you from meeting...

Save this for later.

captions.linkedin:
A single missed LinkedIn message in 2014 can ripple into a career‑long setback, reshaping opportunities you never imagined.

We tend to picture cause and effect as tidy arrows on a whiteboard. Reality, however, prefers tiny nudges—a typo, a wrong train, a misplaced “bless you”—that set off chains we barely notice.

Your trajectory isn’t usually derailed by one dramatic failure. It’s more often a slow‑motion shift: ignoring a message, being labeled unresponsive, missing a promotion, staying longer in a role that stifles growth, and missing the people who could have opened new doors.

Each small act of procrastination or half‑hearted honesty adds a hidden load. Over time that load reshapes the work you produce, nudging you toward shortcuts that feel inevitable.

Recognizing the pattern is only the first step. Insight without agency leaves us with a richer vocabulary for the same old frustration. The challenge is to turn those tiny ripples into deliberate currents.

Resilience. It’s the word productivity gurus love to weaponize. They sell it as this shimmering, ethereal quality—a sort of spiritual elasticity that allows you to bounce back from catastrophe with a smile and a fresh green smoothie. They frame it as "bending like a willow," which sounds lovely until you realize the willow is only bending because something heavy is crushing its soul.

As a professional failure expert, I find the same rhetoric exhausting. The idea that we should "flow" like a river suggests a certain grace. But rivers aren’t graceful; they’re relentless. A river doesn’t "adapt" to a mountain; it spends ten thousand years grinding the mountain into dust out of sheer, stubborn persistence. That’s not resilience. That’s an attrition war.

If you want to actually survive the wreckage of your own decisions—or the random cruelty of the universe—you have to stop trying to "bounce back." Bouncing implies you return to your original shape. Here is the secret: the original shape was flawed. That version of you was the one who walked right into the wall. Why on earth would you want to go back to being that person?

captions.linkedin:
Resilience isn’t a glossy buzzword; it’s the scar you learn to wear. The guru‑crafted promise of “bouncing back” sounds nice until you realize it asks you to return to a broken version of yourself.

The metaphor of a willow bending under weight is seductive, but the tree is only pliant because something heavy is crushing its core. As a failure specialist I see the same rhetoric as a tired song. Rivers don’t flow gracefully; they grind mountains into dust through relentless persistence. That is not resilience—it is an attrition war.

True resilience does not mean restoring the original shape. The original shape was the one that walked into the wall. Instead, it means accepting permanent dents and weaving scar tissue into the design.

Consider objects built to last. We prize seamless, factory‑new surfaces, yet the most compelling beauty lies in the repair. A wound closes, leaving a ridge; that ridge is where the same mistake cannot repeat. The stitching process—slow, methodical, pulling frayed edges together—creates something denser and tougher than the original fabric.

Cultivating this kind of resilience means dropping the performance of “wellness.” Stop trying to be a river for a moment and simply sit with the disaster. Let the failure be cold and uncomfortable. The moment you cease fighting the fact that you’ve been wrecked is the moment you begin to adapt, finding strength not in victory but in the quiet after defeat.

There's this beautiful irony about vulnerability that most people miss until they've already screwed something up so spectacularly that there's nothing left but honesty.

We spend our entire lives building walls—metaphorical ones, obviously, unless you're literally an architect—and then we act surprised when those same walls become prisons. The moment someone tells you "just be vulnerable," your first instinct isn't trust. It's what if I'm wrong? Which, frankly, you probably will be. That's kind of the point.

Here's what nobody warns you: vulnerability doesn't feel like courage at first. It feels like incompetence. You put yourself out there—the idea, the feeling, the half-baked thesis you've been turning over since 3 AM—and the world looks back at you with the blank expression of someone who has absolutely no interest in your inner life. And for one horrible second, you think: this is exactly why I don't do this.

But here's the thing about failure as a teacher (yes, it teaches, everyone says that, bear with me). When you're willing to be bad at something—to let the raw, unpolished version of whatever you're making exist without apology—that's where actual originality hides. Not in perfection. Perfection is just fear wearing a nice outfit.

I learned the hard way that letting my kids experiment online, even when they mess up, is the fastest path to real digital resilience.

We spend years building digital fences—parental controls, strict schedules—only to find they become cages. When a teacher says “just be open online,” my first thought is, “what if they’re wrong?” And often they are. That’s the point.

Vulnerability online doesn’t feel brave at first; it feels like exposing a mistake. You share a photo, a comment, a draft project, and the response can be a blank stare or a quick dismissal. For a moment you think, “this is why I should keep them hidden.”

But failure is a teacher. When a child posts something imperfect and owns it, that’s where genuine learning happens. Perfection is just fear dressed up as safety.
